title: The Shelf Label Habit. How Unit Prices Ended an Argument With Myself
body: For years I bought the same olive oil by the simple method of grabbing the bottle my hand recognized. Then a budgeting app told me I had spent more on oil than on electricity, and I did not believe it, and I checked, and the app was right, and the shelf label was about to change how I shop for everything. Every Israeli supermarket prints a small unit price next to the big one. Shekels per liter, per kilo, per sheet. Most people, I now realize, walk past it the way I did, the way you walk past a fire extinguisher. The big price is for the decision. The small price is for the truth. The truth was that my recognized bottle cost forty percent more per liter than a plainer bottle two shelves down, made by a company whose oil had won the same award, from the same region, in a uglier bottle. The unit price habit is thirty seconds per aisle and it exposes the whole quiet carnival of packaging. The big tub is usually cheaper per gram, except when it is not, and it is almost never cheaper when there is a promotion sticker on it. The sticker is not a unit price. The sticker is a mood. Sale tags glow warm colors for a reason, and the reason is that nobody in the history of shopping has ever felt warmly about shekels per hundred grams. My own biases were the bigger discovery. I believed brands I grew up with were reliably fair. The label showed they were reliably forty percent more. I believed bigger was always better value. The label showed the middle size is often priced as bait, the small size as punishment, the large size as the trap for people who learned the small lesson but not the lesson. I believed rice was rice. The label made rice a category with a spread wide enough to fund a small vacation. There are honest limits to the habit, and I keep them, because a person who computes unit prices at the egg shelf has stopped shopping and started conserving. Freshness beats arithmetic. The cheaper per liter oil that sits half used for a year is more expensive than the one you finish. Time is a unit price too. The habit is for staples, the repeat buys, the things you purchase on autopilot, and autopilot is exactly where the margin lives. The strangest effect was on my sense of the whole store. Once you read unit prices for a month, you can feel pricing the way you feel weather. You know which chain is quietly expensive in dairy and competitive in produce. You know the wholesale pulse of the week, which days the vegetables turn over. Shopping became less emotional, not more calculating. The argument with myself at every shelf, the should I, the what if the cheap one is worse, is over. The label answers first, calmly, in small gray numbers. The app no longer scolds me about oil. The yearly saving across staples is real but not dramatic, and that is the honest summary. The habit will not buy you an apartment. What it bought me was the end of a low hum of doubt that ran under every purchase. I know what a liter costs now. The shelf can shout all it wants. I read the quiet line underneath.
